All the data that I have at my disposal I have shown in an objective manner as best I could. So I provided the information in good faith as evidence that I hoped would be of assistance to this Tribunal, as impartial evidence. Maybe I have made some genuine errors, but none that I have noticed so far. And I have acted in good faith as in all other activities that I perform either before this Tribunal or in other courts or in negotiations with other states. That is a clearly stated position within these agencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, you had mentioned in relation, I believe to an initiative that you took at a meeting with Serbia and Montenegro, and a document was signed defining the question of missing persons, and you had mentioned before that, I believe, in that context that you wanted the abuse of the figures to be stopped. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to explain in a few words. The problem of missing persons is not only the problem of Croatia but also a problem shared by Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia and Montenegro. Very often, figures of missing persons were used to promote political agendas of the day and that has armed the entire process. We have faced situations when some NGOs, later supported by politicians, came out with figures of missing persons, persons let's say Serbs in Croatia, of 4, 5, or 6.000. Even the deputy Prime Minister, Mr. Lajic, came out with a number of Serbs sought by Serbia and Montenegro in Croatia of 2.500. That's the information he had. In order to put a stop to this, I went to a meeting in Belgrade, and that was confirmed at another meeting in Zagreb, where it was agreed that the numbers of missing persons have to be agreed, and the criteria have to be similar or the same as criteria used by the international committee. After adopting this joint position, we came out with numbers in keeping with those criteria, and it was established and recorded in the paper that resulted from that meeting that territorially speaking, 1.140 persons are still sought for, and they are registered in the office for missing persons, and 915 persons went missing in the Operations Flash and Storm, whereas 500 persons are sought in Croatia by Serbia and Montenegro. So on the territory of Croatia, 2.400 persons are missing. We invested that effort in order to remove this whole issue out of the field of politics in order to promote the process of looking for missing persons, and I have presented this evidence to the Court in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you, were persons displaced from the territory of the SAO-K only or also from outside of the SAO-K?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we talk about the displaced persons -- I don't know if I understood your question correctly, but we have discussed three categories of persons who left their homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I'm talking about specifically the SAO-K. Was that the only territory from which persons were displaced as far as your information disclosed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said in my presentation that according to my information, around 30.000 people - that's an estimate - changed their place of residence and they of moved to area not afflicted by the war. For example to Osijek which was not occupied a certain amount of people went to Pula. Some people from Pula --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I think you have answered my question. You said in answer to Defence counsel that essentially this is the substance of it. Whether or not you use counties or municipalities, the numbers that you have produced would come out to the same. Why did you give that answer?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand your question. What exactly did I say in my reply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: My recollection is that you were asked -- well, you were being questioned about the fact that in 1991, municipalities existed, whereas now counties existed, and it was being suggested that your figures might not be correct because of the fact that you didn't address the issue through municipalities as opposed to counties, but you answered that whether or not which one you applied the figures would be the same. Why did you give that answer I want to know. Or did I misunderstand your answer?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you did not misunderstand. Whatever principle we use, whatever territorial principle we use, the numbers have to remain the same. I'll try to clarify on a small example. If we talk about, let's say, Beli Manastir municipality, it belongs to the Osijek-Baranja county. So it is part of the county that has been taken into account in my numbers, because according to the territorial division, the territorial units were smaller. Several of them were united into a county, and when I talk about a county, I talk about the entire county. But only one small part of if was occupied, and from that occupied part those 220.000 were expelled. So the numbers have to tally. I know where the confusion comes from. Distinguished Defence counsel said that a certain number of people were registered as living there, and it's a small number than the ones that I quoted, but it's either that not all the territories were taken into account or some other reason, but there is a logical explanation. If we know that one-third of the territory of Croatia was occupied and there were 4 million and something population, one-third of the population has to be a million or something. It can't be 70.000. The population of one-third of Croatia cannot be 70.000. That is what creates confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm most grateful to you. Thank you, Mr. Grujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, I think it was yesterday or could it be day before yesterday, I'm not sure now, you said that in compiling the list of the killed people you used information from the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, and then you went on to say these lists were unified, and the number of exhumed persons was added to that list. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does this then mean that the lists from the minister -- from the two ministries contain the number of persons whose bodies had already been found and therefore without doubt were not among the persons exhumed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I understood your question correctly, but that number includes all persons about whom we knew that they were dead. Some we had information they were members of armed forces killed in combat, and they were on the list of the Ministry of Defence. We had another list from the Ministry of Health that some persons were killed in areas close to the battlefield or otherwise as a result of combat, and this data flowed into the Ministry of Health where it was aggregated. And the third source were exhumations, persons we -- or, rather, bodies we exhumed and identified. So we integrated the records of soldiers from the Ministry of Defence; the records of persons killed as a result of armed conflict, through hospitals; and the bodies we identified. But 580 mortal remains still remain identified [as interpreted], and they are still not included in any lists. But we still have 580 dead people from the period 1991 to 1995 who are not identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me put my question slightly differently. How did you determine that the exhumed persons whom you added to the list from the ministries were not already mentioned in the ministries' lists so that you avoid duplication?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All records have been cross-checked several times. That was precisely why the government of Croatia gave a mandate to my office to integrate all the records, because the same persons were sometimes recorded both on the list of Ministry of Defence and Ministry of Health. Why? Because reports were sent from localities along two channels, one towards the Ministry of Health and one to the Ministry of Defence. So those lists included also some persons who met a violent death as a result of armed conflict but could not be placed in that context because they were killed in Bosnia, for instance. And that's why the decision was made to sort of clean-out all those lists so that we have a clear picture. And when we identified the bodies from exhumations, we put them only the same list and verified for repetitions. So the list was checked by computer cross-checking, and the second was by manual cross-checking of every name and surname.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We've gone beyond the time for taking the break. We will take the break and come back at half past twelve. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, on Exhibit 300, you gave a list of names of people who you said were in concentration camps. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why -- why are those places called concentration camps?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those places we call in the Croatian version prisons and camps, not concentration camps. This is just the translation. In the Croatian version, in my report this number is said to have been kept in prisons and camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And by "camps," I believe you mean detention camps of some sort, detention units?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Those are places which are not real prisons but are, rather, places in which detainees were held. They were usually in farm buildings such as barns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On Exhibit 309, I don't know whether it can be found quickly, there is a question on that list and the questionnaire relates to Andrija Likic. Do you remember being asked about him yesterday or the other day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, Andrija Likic is listed on that list as a male, and yet he's given a maiden name. Could that be a mistake?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is probably his mother's maiden name. I would have to see this, but I believe this is probably a reference to the maiden name of his mother. When filling in the form, this is probably what was understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe if that exhibit can be shown, because the impression that the Chamber got in looking at those lists was that the particulars therein contained were the particulars of the person about whom the questionnaire was, not about the person's parents. So the understanding by the Chamber was that a maiden name was given to -- a maiden name of the person about whom the questionnaire was. If we could get it on the monitor, please. We have it on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Pardon. We have that name on the monitor. Could we go to the item that talks about maiden name. I'm not able to read in B/C/S which item this will be, but as we can see, at number 9 he's circled as a male. Now, which one is maiden name here? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, under number 8, it's exactly as I said in my previous reply. The question under number 8 is "Mother's maiden name." The previous question, number 7, is "Mother's name," and it says "Katarina." Number 8 is "Mother's maiden name." That's "Krivajic." 9 is "Sex," "Male."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies. Thank you very much. Now, this morning during cross-examination you were asked quite a number of questions relating to some people that you said had not been included in the list of the 12.078 killed, and some of those questions related to missing people, to dead people. What I do want to find out from you is, do you have a comprehensive number that gives all missing people, irrespective of how they went missing, whether they are dead, exhumed, detained. Do you have a comprehensive number of all people that according to your research were affected or don't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no unified statistics because these are different categories. Missing persons need not necessarily be dead. We do believe that most of the missing persons are dead, but we cannot say that until it has been confirmed. Also, persons who were imprisoned and who are released are still alive. So people were victimised by being imprisoned but they have been released. The persons listed as dead are those persons whom we have established beyond any doubt to be dead. We can think that a large number of persons currently listed as missing will eventually end up on the list of dead persons, but that will happen only once they are identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that's fine. That satisfies my query. We shall relate it to the question that was put to you. Thank you very much. That's all I wanted to ask you, Mr. Grujic. Any questions arising from the questions from the Bench? Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: None from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, in connection with a question put to you with respect to the municipalities mentioned in the indictment, when you were asked to compare them with counties, in your view all the municipalities which belonged to the SAO Krajina which are listed in the indictment and about which you were asked by His Honour, they belong to the Lika-Sinj, Karlovac-Sibenik, Knin-Zadar [Realtime transcript read in error "Knin"], and Sisak-Moslavina counties. That was your reply.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat what I said. I said that I think that's how it is but that I cannot be absolutely certain. I said that I think that those towns either belonged to that municipality or border it. I said that more than half of the territory that was occupied has not been included in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, a simple adding up of the figures found in graph number 6 in Exhibit 299, which contains an analysis of displaced persons as it says here --

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Going back to the testimony earlier, my learned colleague summarised it as follows: He said they belonged to the Sibenik, Knin, and Moslavina counties. That was your reply. My learned colleague has missed out Zadar county or nearby was also mentioned, and again I would emphasise that the witness has responded to the best of his ability and has mentioned that he was uncertain as to some of -- exactly where the lines were. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't understand what the objection is about. As I said, I have listed the Lika-Sinj county, the Karlovac county, the Sibenik-Knin county, the Zadar county, and the Sisak-Moslavina county. Those are the ones mentioned by Mr. Grujic in response to Judge Hoepfel's questions. When you add up the figures on page 6 listed next to these counties you arrived at about 105.000 expellees, as the witness calls them. That's simple arithmetic, adding up the numbers mentioned by the expert in his description of the counties. What I'm interested in is whether the expert can explain to us how it comes about that the number of expelled persons, that is 105.000 is possible when in the census from 1991 that the Prosecutor relies on says that there was 78.000 Croats in the population of these areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: These 105.000 that you refer to, are they Croats? Or did the witness say these are Croats?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I expect the witness to respond to what persons at the thinks were expelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But then there is no basis for your question. Until you know whether the witness has said these 105 are Croats, you can't put the question that how does he come to 105 when the Croats were 78.000. You have made no basis for your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness spoke about expulsions. I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness tell us what ethnicity this figure of 105.000 refers to that's mentioned for these five counties?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the addendum I provided the ethnicity of all expellees. This is not, however, broken down by county. I have answered this question more than once. I have nothing more to add to what I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Grujic, thank you very much for coming to testify. This brings us to the end of your testimony. You are excused. You may stand down. Once again, the Chamber thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You want to catch up on time. You may carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Simply that my colleague Mr. Black will be examining the next witness, and may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You want to be excused.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: At the present time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are excused.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is Dr. Davor Strinovic. If he could be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May Dr. Davor Strinovic please be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Strinovic. Thank you for coming. I know you speak English very well, but you've elected to testify in your own first language, Croatian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you receiving the translation properly? Are you hearing my words being translated into your language now?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. All is in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Even though you may understand some of my questions in English, I'd ask you to just please wait until they're translated into your language before you answer. That will allow the interpretation to complete and it will make everyone's life a little easier. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And if at any time you don't understand one of my questions, please just say so and I'll try to state it more clearly. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: First a couple of questions about your professional background. Where are you currently employed, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm employed at the institute of forensic medicine and criminology at the Faculty of Medicine of the University of Zagreb as an associate professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In December of 1991, did you become a member of the Croatian Government Commission for Detainees and Missing Persons?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could you briefly explain the mission of that commission, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Initially meaning from 1991 or early 1992, the basic aim of the commission was to gather information about missing persons and to communicate with all other parties interested in this issue in order to resolve the problems as successfully as possible. Until 1995, the commission had the task of gathering information, holding meetings, and preparing for the work that was to follow after 1995. From 1995 onwards, work in the field began. Exhumations of graves began, both mass graves and individual graves, followed by identification and everything else connected with this job.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What role have you yourself played in the work of the commission since 1991?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: From 1991 to 1995, I was a member of the commission as a doctor and a forensic specialist, and as a person who was able to put questions having to do with issues of missing persons, possible identifications, possible grave locations, grave sites and so on. After 1995, in the government commission for detainees and missing persons, I became the coordinator for the medical part of the work in the field. This means preparing exhumations, exhumations, identification, processing mortal remains, and everything else necessary in order to complete identification and establishing the cause of death of all persons found in graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you personally participate in exhumations and examinations, or did you supervise them or both?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I can say I did both. I attended a certain number of exhumations, and I let other colleagues do others so that I was in charge of coordinating the work even when I wasn't physically present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you still a member of the commission today?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Doctor, you are a forensic pathologist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could you briefly explain what it is that a forensic pathologist does? Just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: A forensic pathologist -- I assume that your questioning is linked to wartime and times following a war. Am I right in assuming that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. Please focus on what a forensic pathologist would have done since 1991 in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Forensic specialists are experts who deal with all kinds of violent death, whereas pathologists deal with diseases. Forensic doctors in cases of disasters, such as air crashes, railway accidents where there are large numbers of victims and identification is difficult, they process the remains and identify the victims in such cases. I wish to point out that forensic medical specialists are trained to do this kind of work, so that from 1991 onwards they carried out post-mortems on the vast majority of all those killed in the Republic of Croatia who died a violent death. They also carried out exhumation and identification of persons who were in graves for a certain period of time. The task of a forensic medical specialist is to carry out a post-mortem, to establish all the features on the body which might be of importance to a court later on. For example, they can describe the clothing, other objects found on the body, what was found on the body, what kind of injuries or other conditions, previous illnesses, deformities or injuries that might have occurred previously, all this in order to later establish the cause of death and the identity of the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. You've mentioned both identification and determination of cause of death. My questions will focus for the most part on determining cause of death. First, how is a cause of death established in a typical case if there is such a thing as a typical case?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Cause of death is one of the hardest problems that a forensic faces on his job, bearing in mind that most of those people were in the grave for a long time after death and the processing of the body is usually done only after exhumation. In view of the large number of fatalities, especially in 1995 onwards, after the exhumations began, accompanied by forensic work, the focus of our work was on the identification of those bodies, and we always tried, when possible, to establish the cause of death. As time went on, the level of our equipment improved. More time was available to devote to establishing the cause of death, certain experience had been acquired, and therefore, the cases processed later, that means after 1995, have the cause of death established with greater precision. It is noteworthy that the sophistication of equipment available to the identification team has a great importance, especially when it comes to establishing the cause of death, because in those cases when the beginning of the post-mortem was marked by taking X-rays that could show the presence of metal objects such as projectiles or parts thereof, and especially shrapnel, which are very difficult to find by post-mortem, were very easy to detect in this way. After this examination by radiologists, the forensic medical doctor starts his work establishing damage on clothing that could be significant and typical of certain injuries. For instance, regular circular defects on several pieces of clothing at the same level indicate a high probability of damage by projectile from a handgun, that is damage by bullet. Irregularly shaped defects of varying sizes and shapes on the clothing are indicative of a different mechanism of damage and are frequently found in the use of shrapnel, blast injuries, et cetera. After this, we move to the examination of skin, if the skin is present, and we have to know that the skin can be preserved for five or more years provided that during the processes this occur after death mummification or saponification is present. Such defects on the skin also indicate with a high degree of probability that these are caused by bullets. Circular defects on the skin indicate injury by bullet. Irregularly shaped, irregular sized defects on the skin may originate from either blasts or other reasons as well, or they can be caused by the use of some other ordnance. After that comes the examination of bone structures and internal organs if preserved. Organs are relatively rarely preserved, although in some cases they exist, and in those cases we can follow the damage done to the organ, and they can also provide indications of the mechanism of injury, be it a gunshot wound or a blast injury, a stab wound, or similar. Most frequently, though, in cases where death occurred several years before exhumation, before the autopsy, the bone structure is preserved. On some bones one can recognise very clearly the instrument that caused damage such as, for instance, the skull. On the skull there are certain regular defects that point with a great certainty to the fact that it was damage by bullet, by projectile, and we see very similar defects on the bones of the pelvis, the chest, the thorax, the shoulder blades. Other bones, depending on the intensity and/or localisation of injuries, may have either regular damage or multiple damage, and in that case it would be very difficult to determine the actual mechanism whereby the damage occurred. In saying so, I mean primarily the long bones of the limbs, the ribs --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, I'm sorry to interrupt you. I have the feeling that you're being very considerate of the interpreters and you're kind of waiting for the interpretation to catch up with you which I'm sure they appreciate. But I just want to encourage you to speak at your normal rhythm. The interpreters are very able and they will keep up with you. So you don't have to slow down for the interpretation too much. If you go too quickly, I'll tell you.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now when we have received the descriptions of all these types of damage, after all that damage has been examined by an anthropologist, which is the case very frequently, the body will be in the stage of putrefication. The bodies will be all mixed up. They will have to be sorted out, and fractures will have to be reconstructed as well as damage so that on the basis of such reconstruction we could make conclusions about the mechanism of injury, be it from a projectile, shrapnel, trauma, et cetera. When we have collected all this data that I have enumerated, together with X-rays, at that stage we can make an estimate with a high degree of certainty of the mechanism of injury. And every forensic doctor who is performing this autopsy will independently determine the cause of death, and he will indicate that the cause of death is certain or possible or probable, or he will indicate that the cause of death is not possible to determine or explain by analysis. So in every -- each one of these categories we get the cause of death as certain or possible or probable or impossible to determine. That would be my briefest possible answer to the question how a forensic doctor determines the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, I'm grateful?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Doctor, I see you keep -- your earphones keep almost falling off and they disturb you. Maybe if you bring them up to over your head they might just be -- hold a little better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's short. It's short. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, thank you for that explanation. Just a very brief question. Is there a difference in technique when determining the cause of death of a person whose -- who died fairly recently as opposed to someone who has been exhumed after several years? Is there any difference in the technique that's used?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just tried to explain the difference that exists, because I was speaking about a typical case where the cause of death was determined several years after death occurred, or, rather, if we are autopsying a bodies just several days after death, the autopsy is much simpler and you can almost always determine the cause of death with great certainty because there are certain vital pre-mortal reactions on the tissues, haemorrhaging, et cetera, and the mechanism of injury, the axis of stabbing or injury, other injury, is very clear. And the autopsy of a fresh corpse is much different in way, and the cause of death can be established with much greater certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And you mentioned that there are cases where a cause of death cannot be ascertained. Is it possible that a person can die a violent death and yet several years later the cause of death cannot be determined based on a forensic examination?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: To our great chagrin, it is possible. That happens. There are cases when we cannot establish the cause of death, that is damage to a soft tissue, damage to the throat, the neck, or to the heart where the person will bleed out but there will be no damage to the bones or there will be no other injury that will remain visible on some other part of the body because the bones are not damaged. Then the cause of death will remain unclear to us, although it will be clear that the death was violent. But we could not ascertain that because we don't have the necessary elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I'm going to move to a slightly different topic now. Did you prepare an expert report for this Tribunal in connection with the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And did you subsequently come here to The Hague to testify in the trial of Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness's expert report has already been admitted in this case by your decision of 13 January 2006, and it is Exhibit 10. I have hard copies with me in case the Chamber would be interested, but otherwise I think there's -- I do not intend to make specific reference to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It might just be helpful if you can give us the copies, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. That's why I brought them. Let me, with the assistance of the usher, please. Your Honour, I have several English copies for the Bench and a copy in B/C/S for the Defence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, by the same decision of 13 January 2006, Dr. Strinovic's Milosevic testimony was also admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis. That testimony has now been uploaded into e-court. It bears two different ERNs because it covered parts of two different days. The ERNs are 05045592 to 5605, and 05045606 to 5693. And, Your Honour, at this point I would ask that they receive a number, please. And it's -- actually, I leave it to the court officer in the court as to whether it should be two numbers or one number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Court will leave it to the court officer to decide. Can you give us an exhibit number or numbers to that report, Mr. Court officer?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be for exhibit -- or for document number 05045592, Exhibit number 321; and for document 05045606, that will be Exhibit number 322.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I don't intend to give a detailed summary of that testimony however I think it's appropriate to very extremely briefly summarise it. In his Milosevic testimony, Dr. Strinovic talked about his work with the government Commission for Detainees and Missing Persons, as well as his qualifications. In addition, a number of documents were tendered into evidence in that case. Those documents prepared by Dr. Strinovic summarised information about the victims at several locations relevant to the Milosevic indictment, including information regarding cause of death. A number of those locations are also relevant to this case, Your Honour, including Skabrnja, Nadin, Bacin, and some other locations. That's all I have to say directly about the Milosevic events.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, before you came here this week to testify in this case, were you asked to prepare some updated materials related to your -- to your expert report?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What specifically were you asked to prepare?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I was asked to follow the list that I received, the list of persons broken down by individual graves, to determine the -- to list the causes of death for those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And did you provide that to the material -- that material to the Prosecution last week? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, this can be done on e-court and perhaps in hard copy as well, I'd like to show the witness ERN 04693958 to 3967. And I have some copies in English as well as in B/C/S for the witness and for Defence counsel. Dr. Strinovic, please just take a moment to look through that document, the different pages, and tell me whether these are the updated materials that you provided last week. Doctor, do you have a copy of these in your own language? I see you're looking at the English there, but do you have a copy in your own language in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And are these the materials that you provided last week?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you prepare these lists yourself?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: With the assistance of a colleague of mine from the institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Where did you obtain the information that's shown on these lists?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: This information is contain in the database of the Institute for Forensic Medicine, and they were uploaded from the protocols that we keep at the institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You mentioned that they were uploaded from the protocols that we keep. Could you be -- could you give a little more information about where the information that's in the database, where that information comes from?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The information that is included in the database comes from protocols of the Institute for Forensic Medicine or in some cases that we get from the government office for cases that were not processed by our institute. We receive such data from the government when we are dealing with a specific grave site.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Doctor, what I would ask of you now is just take us briefly through each of the locations in your list and just briefly summarise the information that is there for each location, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can I start? According to my own sequence or do you have something to suggest?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, please. Any sequence is fine. The way they appear in these documents will be ...

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I have it organised -- well, can we start with Bacin?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually, so that it's easiest to follow, I think the English copy I have begins with Vukovici. Do you mind beginning with Vukovici?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: No problem. I can say the following about Vukovici: The disappearance of persons in that place was registered on the 7th of November, 1991, and the bodies were exhumed on the 13th of August, 1996. Ten bodies were found. Sorry. That was the list of missing persons. There were ten persons on the list of missing persons. In the field, two were autopsied, Vukovic Ivan and Vukovic Nikola, and both causes of death were gunshot wounds. After that, the mortal remains were processed at the Institute for Forensic Medicine, and they were found to belong to at least three persons, because the remains were all mixed up. They were found in the site of a former large fire, and the identity was not established in the cases of these three persons. The cause of death was impossible to ascertain because the fragments of bones were badly burned, and they were too small as they were found. That is one of the cases when it is impossible to perform a positive identification, because the regular methods cannot be applied, and the fragments of bones are so small and so badly burned that it is difficult to establish --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Can we now turn to Lipovaca, which is the next location?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The place is called Lipovaca Dreznica. The persons went missing on the 28th of November, 1991. The bodies were exhumed on the 12th of June, 1996. The processing and identification were carried out in the field. Seven persons were found. All of them were identified. And in the case of all seven persons, it was established that they had gunshot wounds. The late Mirko Brozincevic was found to have no visible traces that might indicate the cause of death, but according to information provided by eyewitnesses who stated that he had been shot through the neck, the pathologist in charge of the autopsy wrote down that the cause of death was a gunshot wound. These are seven persons. The cause of death has been established in six of them being a gunshot wound, whereas in the case of the seventh person the cause of death is based on eyewitness accounts rather than the autopsy itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. In the list under cause of death for Mirko Brozincevic. It says gunshot wounds. When did you determine that was based on information from witnesses rather than from the forensic identification -- forensic examination, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: On reading the pathologist's report, the pathologist who was there. Protocols were not compiled in that time to be sent to the institute but rather a record was taken in the presence of an investigating Judge who dictated into the court record. And it transpired from the court record that the doctor who carried out the autopsy received information which led him to conclude that this was the cause of death. I read this information and I am now conveying it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And just so it's clear, was that on Monday after you'd arrived in The Hague that you had a chance to review this particular protocol?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to review protocols related to the other causes of death indicated in your lists?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you find any other cases, while we're on the topic, that you thought maybe there should be that kind of qualification of the cause of death that's given in the lists?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Not in the case of Lipovacka Dreznica, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If as we go through these various locations you see any other instance like that, please mention it. We'd like to have that information. If you have no further comments on Lipovacka, please turn to Saborsko, the next location.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In Saborsko, the fact that the persons went missing was recorded on the 12th of November, 1991. The bodies were exhumed on the 30th of October, 1995. 28 persons are listed, 24 were autopsied. Of the remaining four, Mate Matovina is listed as dead, which is why he's not on the list, and Leopold Conjar, number 5; Ivanti Cantin [as interpreted], number 6; and Ivan Matovina, number 11, were autopsied in the field and no record was made which is why we did not include the cause of death on this list. Of the 24 persons autopsied, ten had gunshot wounds, probable trauma, one, and the cause of death unascertained in the case of 13. Three unknown persons were also autopsied from the Saborsko location. They were not identified. One had gunshot wounds as the cause of death and the others the cause of death was unknown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Doctor, you said that Mate Matovina was listed as dead, which is why he's not on the list. I see he's number 18 on the list.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, he is on the list. On the list of persons missing in Saborsko. Mate Matovina, the person we are talking about now, is on the list, but he was not found or autopsied, which is why the cause of death is not listed. As for the three other persons I mentioned, they were autopsied. But this was done in the field, which is why we don't have the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see that number 17 is also Mate Matovina. Are there two Mate Matovinas? Were there two Mate Matovinas who are distinct personalities?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Two different persons of two different ages but with the same first and last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, unless you have further comments on the Saborsko location, perhaps we could turn now to Bacin.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In Bacin, the persons were reported as missing in October 1991. They were exhumed from the 13th through the 25th of March, 1997. These are 44 persons who are on the list, and there were a further five from other locations so that there were 49 persons found in Bacin. The causes of death are as followings: 36 gunshot wounds, 4 probably gunshot wounds, two cases explosive wounds, two cases probable explosive wounds, one case of trauma, and unascertained in four cases. I wish to mention that there were a further 14 unidentified persons in Bacin. Of these, seven died of gunshot wounds and the others the cause of death was not ascertained.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This list has 108 people total, of which you've said now how many were exhumed. What about the bodies of the other people? Have those been found?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: We don't know that for now. They have not been identified. Whether they have been found and are listed as unidentified or whether they have not been found at all is something we won't know until all the bodies are identified. As I stated, we have 14 bodies not yet identified. They are probably persons on this list, but we don't know who they are. We autopsied them and they are probably from the Bacin list, but we haven't identified them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Doctor, let's turn now to the Nadin location, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In Nadin, the fact that the persons went missing was recorded on the 19th of November, 1991. Five days later, the bodies were handed over to the Croatian side and autopsied. These were seven persons. In the case of all seven, they died of gunshot wounds. In addition to this list of seven persons, two other persons were autopsied, Marko Zupan, Marija Drazina, in both cases they also died of gunshot wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps we can turn to the next location, Bruska.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In Bruska, the fact that the persons went missing was recorded on the 21st of December, 1991. They were exhumed on the 26th of April, 1996. There are ten persons on the list, nine of whom died of gunshot wounds, and one person, Svetozar Draca, was listed as killed and not autopsied. Another person was exhumed in the Bruska location. That's the Josip Marinovic who went missing on the 10th of June, 1992, and the cause of death was trauma, contusion -- concussion, that is, and lung fracture.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps we can turn to Skabrnja. There are two events. Let's start with the first event in Skabrnja, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The first event in Skabrnja, the fact that the persons went missing was recorded on the 18th and 19th of November, 1991, and the bodies were taken over on the 23rd of November, 1991, when they were autopsied. These were fresh corpses, in other words. There were 28 -- or, rather, 38 persons. 23 of them had gunshot wounds, 11 explosive wounds, one person had trauma, and for three persons there is no information about the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And the second event in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The second event was that persons went missing on the 18th of November, 1991, until February 1992, in this time period, and they were exhumed on the 5th and 6th of June, 1996. There are 26 names on the list. In 15 cases the cause of death were gunshot wounds; in five persons, explosive wounds; trauma in four cases; and in two cases there is no information about the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Your Honours, I would ask that this document receive an exhibit number and be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is received into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 323, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I realise we still have about two minutes. The next short topic involves playing a video, which is about two or three minutes long itself, so I'm afraid it would take us past the hour, Your Honour. It might be a convenient just to stop now and resume in the morning, unless you prefer, I can just push on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you can play it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you're going to play it, our going to ask questions on it. Isn't it better just to play it tomorrow and then follow on with your questions? THE PROSECUTOR: I think that's the best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Unless you want to sit right through.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Now until tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, whenever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's convenient time now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll then adjourn until tomorrow morning. We're coming back to this courtroom at 9.00 in the morning -- I beg your pardon. We're going to Courtroom I in terms of the arrangements we made this morning. Yes. Courtroom I tomorrow morning at 9.00. Court adjourned.
